concept.name: Latency
concept.definition: The time delay between a market event and a participant's ability to observe and act on it - quoted in the CFTC's automated-trading concept release from Hasbrouck and Saar as the time it takes to learn about an event (e.g., a change in the bid), generate a response, and have the exchange act on the response.
concept.intuition: It is the lag between something happening in the market and your reaction actually landing at the exchange.
concept.mechanics: Latency decomposes into market-data dissemination, network transit, decision logic, and exchange processing; participants reduce it through co-location, direct exchange data feeds, microwave networks, and streamlined code, with competitive levels now in microseconds.
concept.failure_modes: Latency differentials let faster participants pick off slower resting orders after price moves, and average latency figures hide the tail spikes that dominate adverse outcomes in fast markets.
concept.misconceptions: Minimal latency matters mainly for market making, arbitrage, and aggressive execution strategies; most investors are economically indifferent to microsecond differences.
concept.example: A trader whose system reacts 100 microseconds slower than competitors is systematically picked off when a correlated instrument moves first.

citations.source: CFTC, Concept Release on Risk Controls and System Safeguards for Automated Trading Environments, 78 FR 56542
citations.section: Part II.A.2 Advances in High-Speed Communication Networks and Reductions in Latency (incl. note 18, Hasbrouck-Saar definition)
